questions.question: What are the three GC generations in .NET and what is their purpose?
options: Gen 0, 1, 2 — they separate objects by size
Gen 0, 1, 2 — they separate objects by age, collecting short-lived objects more frequently
Gen A, B, C — they separate objects by type
There is only one generation in Unity's Mono runtime
questions.explanation: Gen 0 holds new short-lived objects and is collected most often. Objects that survive a collection are promoted to Gen 1, then Gen 2. This avoids scanning long-lived objects on every collection. Note: Unity's older Mono backend uses Boehm GC which is non-generational, but IL2CPP on newer Unity versions supports incremental GC.
questions.hint: New objects go in Gen 0. Survivors get promoted. Higher generations are collected less often.

questions.question: What is the purpose of implementing `IDisposable`?
options: To make objects eligible for garbage collection
To provide deterministic cleanup of unmanaged resources
To prevent the GC from collecting the object
To mark the object as readonly
questions.explanation: IDisposable.Dispose() lets you release unmanaged resources (file handles, native memory, database connections) immediately rather than waiting for the GC finalizer. Use it with 'using' statements for automatic cleanup.
questions.hint: The GC handles managed memory. File handles, sockets, and native memory need manual cleanup.

questions.question: What does the `using` statement guarantee for an IDisposable object?
options: The object is never garbage collected
Dispose is called when the block exits, even if an exception is thrown
The object is immediately freed from memory
The object is shared across threads safely
questions.explanation: The using statement compiles into a try/finally that calls Dispose in the finally block. This ensures cleanup happens regardless of exceptions.

questions.question: Why should finalizers (~ClassName) be avoided in most cases?
options: Finalizers prevent the class from being instantiated
Objects with finalizers survive an extra GC cycle and are collected non-deterministically on a separate thread
Finalizers cause compile errors in Unity
Finalizers are called immediately when the object goes out of scope
questions.explanation: The GC places finalizable objects on a finalization queue instead of collecting them immediately. They survive to the next generation, and the finalizer runs on a separate thread at an unpredictable time. Prefer IDisposable for cleanup.

questions.question: What is `Span<T>` used for?
options: Allocating managed arrays on the heap
Providing a safe, allocation-free view over contiguous memory
Replacing List<T> for dynamic collections
Enabling multithreaded access to arrays
questions.explanation: Span<T> is a ref struct that provides a type-safe view over arrays, stack memory (stackalloc), or native memory without allocating. It enables slicing and processing data without copying.
questions.hint: It is a ref struct that wraps a pointer and a length — no copying, no allocating.

questions.question: What does `stackalloc` do?
options: Allocates memory on the heap with a stack-like lifetime
Allocates a block of memory on the stack, avoiding GC entirely
Creates a new thread stack
Allocates memory that persists across method calls
questions.explanation: stackalloc allocates a block of memory on the stack frame. It's freed automatically when the method returns. Combined with Span<T>, it enables zero-allocation temporary buffers. Be cautious with large allocations — stack space is limited.
questions.hint: Stack memory is freed when the method returns. No GC involved.

questions.question: Why is calling `GC.Collect()` manually generally discouraged?
options: It does nothing at runtime
It forces a full collection which causes a frame spike and disrupts the GC's internal optimisation heuristics
It only works in the editor
It permanently disables automatic collection
questions.explanation: Manual GC.Collect() triggers a full blocking collection across all generations, causing a noticeable frame spike. It also resets the GC's adaptive budgets. Only use it at non-critical moments like scene loading screens.
questions.hint: A full collection pauses everything to scan all generations.

questions.question: Why do lambda closures that capture local variables cause heap allocations?
options: Lambdas always run on a background thread
The compiler generates a class to hold the captured variables, which is allocated on the heap
Local variables are copied into a new array
Closures disable the garbage collector
questions.explanation: When a lambda captures a local variable, the compiler creates a hidden class (display class) to store it. An instance of this class is heap-allocated. In hot paths, this creates GC pressure. Avoid captures in performance-critical code.
questions.hint: The compiler generates a hidden class (display class) to hold captured variables.

questions.question: What is string interning in .NET?
options: Compressing strings to save memory
Storing one copy of each unique string literal in a shared pool so identical literals reference the same object
Converting strings to byte arrays
Encrypting strings at compile time
questions.explanation: The CLR automatically interns string literals — identical compile-time strings share the same reference. Runtime-created strings are not interned by default unless you call string.Intern(). This saves memory but the intern pool is never garbage collected.
questions.hint: The CLR keeps a pool of string literals. "hello" == "hello" is a reference comparison that passes.

questions.question: What is the Large Object Heap (LOH)?
options: A heap for objects larger than 85,000 bytes that is only collected during Gen 2 collections and is not compacted by default
A special heap for strings only
A heap that is collected every frame
A heap for static objects
questions.explanation: Objects 85,000+ bytes go on the LOH. It is only collected during full Gen 2 collections and is not compacted by default, which can lead to memory fragmentation. Avoid frequent large array allocations. Note: this applies to .NET — Unity's Boehm GC does not have an LOH, but IL2CPP builds on newer platforms may use a different allocator.
questions.hint: Objects over 85KB go to a special heap that is rarely collected and never compacted by default.
